```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.2,
  dpi = 110
```

This article uses banditlab on a radio access network (RAN) problem:
choosing the modulation and coding scheme (MCS) for a 5G NR downlink
user. It compares bandit policies with two baselines that a network
engineer would recognise: a static CQI-to-MCS rule and outer-loop link
adaptation (OLLA).

It also demonstrates the parts of banditlab that matter most for
telecoms work: custom environments (`bandit_custom()` and a new
environment class), custom policies through the three-method extension
API, seed-paired comparisons, and what the package cannot yet do.

> **Scope.** Everything here is a simulation. The link model is a
> deliberately simple abstraction (described below) chosen so that the
> true expected reward of every arm is known and regret can be computed
> exactly. The results show how the policies behave under this model;
> they are not field measurements and should not be quoted as expected
> gains on a live network.

```{r setup}
library(banditlab)
library(ggplot2)
```

## 1. The decision problem

At each transmission opportunity the scheduler picks an MCS. A higher
MCS carries more bits per resource element but is more likely to fail
decoding (a NACK). The useful quantity is the *delivered* spectral
efficiency: the MCS spectral efficiency if the block is decoded, and
zero otherwise.

The arms are eight entries of the NR PDSCH MCS table for up to 64QAM
(3GPP TS 38.214, Table 5.1.3.1-1). Values are spectral efficiency in
bit/s/Hz.

```{r mcs}
se <- c(MCS0 = 0.2344, MCS4 = 0.6016, MCS8 = 1.1758, MCS12 = 1.6953,
        MCS16 = 2.5703, MCS20 = 3.6094, MCS24 = 4.8164, MCS27 = 5.5547)
se_max <- max(se)
```

### Link model

* Per-opportunity SINR is Gaussian in dB around the user's mean SINR,
  with a standard deviation of 3 dB (a stand-in for fast fading and
  interference fluctuation).
* Each MCS has a decoding threshold from an attenuated Shannon bound,
  $\text{SINR}_m = 10\log_{10}\!\left(2^{\,\text{SE}_m/\eta} - 1\right)$
  with $\eta = 0.75$.
* The probability of an ACK is a logistic curve in the gap between the
  realised SINR and the threshold, with slope 1.5 per dB.
* The reward is delivered spectral efficiency normalised to `[0, 1]`:
  $r = \mathbb{1}\{\text{ACK}\}\,\text{SE}_m / \text{SE}_{\max}$.

The expected reward of each arm is computed by numerical integration,
so banditlab can report exact pseudo-regret.

```{r link-model}
eta <- 0.75
slope <- 1.5
sigma_db <- 3
threshold_db <- 10 * log10(2^(se / eta) - 1)

p_ack <- function(sinr_db, mcs) {
  1 / (1 + exp(-slope * (sinr_db - threshold_db[[mcs]])))
}

expected_reward <- function(mean_sinr_db) {
  vapply(names(se), function(m) {
    ack <- integrate(
      function(s) p_ack(s, m) * dnorm(s, mean_sinr_db, sigma_db),
      mean_sinr_db - 8 * sigma_db, mean_sinr_db + 8 * sigma_db
    )$value
    ack * se[[m]] / se_max
  }, numeric(1))
}

draw_reward <- function(mcs, mean_sinr_db) {
  sinr <- rnorm(1, mean_sinr_db, sigma_db)
  ack <- runif(1) < p_ack(sinr, mcs)
  as.numeric(ack) * se[[mcs]] / se_max
}

round(threshold_db, 1)
```

Three users represent the cell edge, the middle of the cell and the
cell centre. Each has a different best MCS:

```{r scenarios}
scenarios <- c(cell_edge = 5, mid_cell = 12, cell_centre = 18)
mu_table <- sapply(scenarios, expected_reward)
round(mu_table, 3)
apply(mu_table, 2, function(x) names(which.max(x)))
```

## 2. Environments

`bandit_custom()` wraps the sampler. Supplying `expected_rewards` turns
on regret metrics.

```{r envs}
make_env <- function(mean_sinr_db) {
  bandit_custom(
    sampler = function(arm) draw_reward(arm, mean_sinr_db),
    arms = names(se),
    expected_rewards = expected_reward(mean_sinr_db)
  )
}
envs <- lapply(scenarios, make_env)
envs$cell_edge
```

## 3. Baselines written with the extension API

Both baselines are ordinary banditlab policies: a constructor and three
S3 methods. Neither required any change to the package.

### Static CQI rule

The UE reports a wideband CQI; the rule picks the highest MCS whose
threshold is below the reported SINR. CQI reports are often optimistic,
so the rule is given a +3 dB reporting bias.

```{r static-rule}
policy_static_rule <- function(reported_sinr_db) {
  structure(list(reported_sinr_db = reported_sinr_db),
            class = c("static_rule_policy", "bandit_policy"))
}
pick_mcs <- function(sinr_db) {
  ok <- names(threshold_db)[threshold_db <= sinr_db]
  if (length(ok) == 0) names(threshold_db)[1] else ok[length(ok)]
}
policy_state.static_rule_policy <- function(policy, arms, ...) {
  policy$arms <- arms
  policy$choice <- pick_mcs(policy$reported_sinr_db)
  policy
}
select_arm.static_rule_policy <- function(policy, t, ...) {
  list(arm = policy$choice, propensity = 1, reason = "cqi_table")
}
update_state.static_rule_policy <- function(policy, arm, reward, t, ...) {
  policy
}
```

### Outer-loop link adaptation (OLLA)

OLLA is the standard industry mechanism. It adds an offset to the
reported SINR: down by `step_down` dB on a NACK, up by
`step_down * target / (1 - target)` dB on an ACK, which drives the
block error rate (BLER) to `target` (10% here). A positive reward means
the block was decoded, so the policy can read ACK/NACK from the reward.

```{r olla}
policy_olla <- function(reported_sinr_db, target_bler = 0.1, step_down = 0.5) {
  structure(
    list(reported_sinr_db = reported_sinr_db, target_bler = target_bler,
         step_down = step_down,
         step_up = step_down * target_bler / (1 - target_bler)),
    class = c("olla_policy", "bandit_policy")
  )
}
policy_state.olla_policy <- function(policy, arms, ...) {
  policy$arms <- arms
  policy$offset <- 0
  policy
}
select_arm.olla_policy <- function(policy, t, ...) {
  list(arm = pick_mcs(policy$reported_sinr_db + policy$offset),
       propensity = 1, reason = "olla")
}
update_state.olla_policy <- function(policy, arm, reward, t, ...) {
  policy$offset <- policy$offset +
    if (reward > 0) policy$step_up else -policy$step_down
  policy
}
```

### Thompson sampling for non-binary rewards

`policy_thompson()` is Beta-Bernoulli and rejects rewards that are not 0
or 1. Delivered spectral efficiency is continuous, so we use the
standard binarisation trick (Agrawal and Goyal, 2012): on reward
$r \in [0, 1]$, update the posterior with a Bernoulli($r$) draw. The
expected update is unchanged, so the policy targets the same arm.

```{r ts-binarised}
policy_thompson_binarised <- function(alpha = 1, beta = 1) {
  structure(list(prior_alpha = alpha, prior_beta = beta),
            class = c("thompson_binarised_policy", "bandit_policy"))
}
policy_state.thompson_binarised_policy <- function(policy, arms, ...) {
  policy$arms <- arms
  policy$alpha <- setNames(rep(policy$prior_alpha, length(arms)), arms)
  policy$beta <- setNames(rep(policy$prior_beta, length(arms)), arms)
  policy
}
select_arm.thompson_binarised_policy <- function(policy, t, ...) {
  draws <- rbeta(length(policy$arms), policy$alpha, policy$beta)
  list(arm = policy$arms[[which.max(draws)]], propensity = NA_real_,
       reason = "posterior_draw")
}
update_state.thompson_binarised_policy <- function(policy, arm, reward, t, ...) {
  b <- as.numeric(runif(1) < reward)
  policy$alpha[[arm]] <- policy$alpha[[arm]] + b
  policy$beta[[arm]] <- policy$beta[[arm]] + 1 - b
  policy
}
```

## 4. Experiment 1: stationary users

Each policy gets 2,000 transmission opportunities, replicated 200 times
with seed-paired random number streams. The static rule and OLLA both
start from the same +3 dB optimistic CQI.

```{r exp1, cache = TRUE}
horizon <- 2000
reps <- 200
cqi_bias_db <- 3

run_scenario <- function(name) {
  sinr <- scenarios[[name]]
  run_experiment(
    envs[[name]],
    policies = list(
      static_rule = policy_static_rule(sinr + cqi_bias_db),
      olla        = policy_olla(sinr + cqi_bias_db),
      eps_greedy  = policy_epsilon_greedy(0.05),
      ucb1        = policy_ucb1(),
      thompson    = policy_thompson_binarised()
    ),
    horizon = horizon,
    replications = reps,
    seed = 2026,
    checkpoints = seq(100, horizon, by = 100)
  )
}
results <- lapply(setNames(names(scenarios), names(scenarios)), run_scenario)
```

### Results

`summary()` gives final cumulative pseudo-regret (in units of
normalised spectral efficiency summed over 2,000 opportunities) and the
share of opportunities spent on the best MCS.

```{r exp1-summary}
summ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(n) {
  s <- as.data.frame(summary(results[[n]]))
  s$scenario <- n
  s
}))
mean_se <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(n) {
  agg <- aggregate(total_reward ~ policy, data = results[[n]]$summary, FUN = mean)
  agg$scenario <- n
  agg
}))
tab <- merge(summ, mean_se, by = c("scenario", "policy"))
tab$mean_delivered_se <- tab$total_reward / horizon * se_max
tab$oracle_se <- max_oracle <- vapply(
  tab$scenario, function(n) max(mu_table[, n]) * se_max, numeric(1)
)
tab$pct_of_oracle <- 100 * tab$mean_delivered_se / tab$oracle_se
names(tab)
```

```{r exp1-table}
show <- tab[, c("scenario", "policy", "mean_delivered_se", "pct_of_oracle",
                grep("regret", names(tab), value = TRUE)[1],
                grep("optimal", names(tab), value = TRUE)[1])]
show[order(show$scenario, -show$pct_of_oracle), ] |>
  transform(mean_delivered_se = round(mean_delivered_se, 3),
            pct_of_oracle = round(pct_of_oracle, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE, digits = 3,
               caption = "Delivered spectral efficiency (bit/s/Hz) and regret, 200 replicates")
```

Cumulative regret over time for the mid-cell user:

```{r exp1-plot}
autoplot(results$mid_cell, metric = "cumulative_regret") +
  labs(subtitle = "Mid-cell user, mean SINR 12 dB, 200 seed-paired replicates")
```

And for the cell centre, where the optimistic CQI hurts the static rule
most:

```{r exp1-plot-centre}
autoplot(results$cell_centre, metric = "cumulative_regret") +
  labs(subtitle = "Cell-centre user, mean SINR 18 dB, 200 seed-paired replicates")
```

Seed-paired differences against OLLA (positive means more regret than
OLLA):

```{r exp1-paired}
paired <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(results), function(n) {
  cmp <- as.data.frame(compare_policies(results[[n]], baseline = "olla"))
  cmp$scenario <- n
  cmp
}))
agg <- aggregate(difference ~ scenario + policy, data = paired,
                 FUN = function(d) c(mean = mean(d),
                                     se = sd(d) / sqrt(length(d))))
agg <- do.call(data.frame, agg)
names(agg)[3:4] <- c("mean_difference", "std_error")
knitr::kable(agg, digits = 2,
             caption = "Paired regret difference versus OLLA at step 2,000")
```

### Reading the results

With `seed = 2026` the run above gives the following picture.

* The **static rule** never learns. With a +3 dB optimistic CQI it sits
  on the wrong MCS for the whole horizon and delivers only
  `r round(tab$pct_of_oracle[tab$scenario == "mid_cell" & tab$policy == "static_rule"])`%
  of the oracle spectral efficiency mid-cell and
  `r round(tab$pct_of_oracle[tab$scenario == "cell_centre" & tab$policy == "static_rule"])`%
  at the cell centre.
* **OLLA** removes the CQI bias quickly and is the strongest policy at
  the cell centre. It converges to the MCS meeting a 10% BLER target,
  which is not the throughput-optimal MCS at the cell edge, where it
  delivers `r round(tab$pct_of_oracle[tab$scenario == "cell_edge" & tab$policy == "olla"])`%
  of the oracle.
* **Thompson sampling** optimises delivered spectral efficiency
  directly. Paired against OLLA it has lower regret at the cell edge
  (`r sprintf("%.1f", agg$mean_difference[agg$scenario == "cell_edge" & agg$policy == "thompson"])`)
  and mid-cell
  (`r sprintf("%.1f", agg$mean_difference[agg$scenario == "mid_cell" & agg$policy == "thompson"])`),
  and slightly higher regret at the cell centre
  (`r sprintf("%+.1f", agg$mean_difference[agg$scenario == "cell_centre" & agg$policy == "thompson"])`).
* **Epsilon-greedy** with 5% exploration does well here because the
  reward model is smooth and low-noise relative to the gaps between
  neighbouring MCS values. That is a property of this model, not a
  general result.
* **UCB1** is the weakest learner. Its exploration bonus,
  $\sqrt{2 \log t / n}$, is calibrated for rewards spanning `[0, 1]`,
  but here the best arm's mean is at most
  `r round(max(mu_table), 2)` and the gaps between good arms are a few
  hundredths, so the bonus dominates and UCB1 over-explores. This is a
  practical warning: reward scaling matters for UCB-type policies.

## 5. Experiment 2: the radio conditions change

Real radio conditions are not stationary. Here the user's mean SINR
falls from 18 dB to 8 dB halfway through (for example, a neighbour
cell's load rises at busy hour). The best MCS changes from MCS20 to
MCS12.

### A time-aware environment

banditlab's `sample_reward()` generic receives only the arm, not the
time step, so a drifting environment must track time itself. The class
below counts calls and wraps at the horizon so every replicate sees the
same schedule. This is a workaround (see Section 6).

```{r drift-env}
bandit_drifting_sinr <- function(sinr_before, sinr_after, change_at, horizon) {
  clock <- new.env()
  clock$n <- 0L
  structure(
    list(arms = names(se), n_arms = length(se), expected_rewards = NULL,
         sinr_before = sinr_before, sinr_after = sinr_after,
         change_at = change_at, horizon = horizon, clock = clock),
    class = c("drifting_sinr_environment", "bandit_environment")
  )
}
sample_reward.drifting_sinr_environment <- function(environment, arm, ...) {
  clk <- environment$clock
  t <- (clk$n %% environment$horizon) + 1L
  clk$n <- clk$n + 1L
  sinr <- if (t < environment$change_at) environment$sinr_before else environment$sinr_after
  draw_reward(arm, sinr)
}
```

Because the expected rewards change over time, the engine cannot
compute regret (it reports `NA`). We keep full trajectories and compute
*dynamic* regret against the time-varying best arm ourselves.

### A policy that forgets: discounted Thompson sampling

Stationary Thompson sampling accumulates evidence forever, so after the
change it keeps trusting MCS20 for a long time. Discounted Thompson
sampling (Raj and Kalyani, 2017) decays every arm's counts by a factor
`gamma` each step, keeping the effective memory around
`1 / (1 - gamma)` observations.

```{r dts}
policy_discounted_thompson <- function(gamma = 0.99, alpha = 1, beta = 1) {
  structure(list(gamma = gamma, prior_alpha = alpha, prior_beta = beta),
            class = c("discounted_thompson_policy", "bandit_policy"))
}
policy_state.discounted_thompson_policy <- function(policy, arms, ...) {
  policy$arms <- arms
  policy$s <- setNames(rep(0, length(arms)), arms)
  policy$f <- setNames(rep(0, length(arms)), arms)
  policy
}
select_arm.discounted_thompson_policy <- function(policy, t, ...) {
  draws <- rbeta(length(policy$arms), policy$s + policy$prior_alpha,
                 policy$f + policy$prior_beta)
  list(arm = policy$arms[[which.max(draws)]], propensity = NA_real_,
       reason = "discounted_posterior_draw")
}
update_state.discounted_thompson_policy <- function(policy, arm, reward, t, ...) {
  b <- as.numeric(runif(1) < reward)
  policy$s <- policy$gamma * policy$s
  policy$f <- policy$gamma * policy$f
  policy$s[[arm]] <- policy$s[[arm]] + b
  policy$f[[arm]] <- policy$f[[arm]] + 1 - b
  policy
}
```

OLLA here uses the CQI reported at the start (18 dB + 3 dB bias) and
must track the change through its offset alone; a real scheduler would
also receive new CQI reports, so this baseline is pessimistic for OLLA.

```{r exp2, cache = TRUE}
change_at <- 1001
reps2 <- 100
env_drift <- bandit_drifting_sinr(18, 8, change_at, horizon)

res2 <- run_experiment(
  env_drift,
  policies = list(
    olla        = policy_olla(18 + cqi_bias_db),
    ucb1        = policy_ucb1(),
    thompson    = policy_thompson_binarised(),
    dts_0.99    = policy_discounted_thompson(gamma = 0.99),
    dts_0.998   = policy_discounted_thompson(gamma = 0.998)
  ),
  horizon = horizon,
  replications = reps2,
  seed = 2026,
  keep_trajectories = TRUE
)
```

```{r exp2-regret}
mu_before <- expected_reward(18)
mu_after <- expected_reward(8)
tr <- as.data.frame(res2$trajectories)
after <- tr$step >= change_at
tr$mu_arm <- ifelse(after, mu_after[tr$arm], mu_before[tr$arm])
tr$mu_best <- ifelse(after, max(mu_after), max(mu_before))
tr$inst_regret <- tr$mu_best - tr$mu_arm
tr <- tr[order(tr$policy, tr$replicate, tr$step), ]
tr$cum_regret <- ave(tr$inst_regret, tr$policy, tr$replicate, FUN = cumsum)

band <- aggregate(cum_regret ~ policy + step, data = tr[tr$step %% 20 == 0, ],
                  FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x),
                                      lo = unname(quantile(x, 0.1)),
                                      hi = unname(quantile(x, 0.9))))
band <- do.call(data.frame, band)
names(band)[3:5] <- c("mean", "lo", "hi")

ggplot(band, aes(step, mean, colour = policy, fill = policy, linetype = policy)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = change_at, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_banditlab() + scale_fill_banditlab() +
  theme_banditlab() +
  labs(title = "Dynamic cumulative pseudo-regret",
       subtitle = "Mean SINR drops from 18 dB to 8 dB at step 1,001; band = 10th-90th percentile",
       x = "Transmission opportunity", y = "Cumulative pseudo-regret",
       colour = "Policy", fill = "Policy", linetype = "Policy")
```

```{r exp2-table}
final <- tr[tr$step == horizon, ]
phase <- aggregate(inst_regret ~ policy + I(step >= change_at),
                   data = tr, FUN = sum)
names(phase) <- c("policy", "after_change", "regret")
phase$regret <- phase$regret / reps2
wide <- reshape(phase, idvar = "policy", timevar = "after_change",
                direction = "wide")
names(wide) <- c("policy", "regret_before_change", "regret_after_change")
best_after <- names(which.max(mu_after))
share_after <- aggregate(I(arm == best_after) ~ policy,
                         data = tr[tr$step > horizon - 200, ], FUN = mean)
names(share_after)[2] <- "best_mcs_share_last_200"
knitr::kable(merge(wide, share_after), digits = 2,
             caption = "Mean dynamic regret per replicate, by phase")
```

### Reading the results

```{r exp2-numbers, include = FALSE}
w <- setNames(wide$regret_after_change, wide$policy)
b <- setNames(wide$regret_before_change, wide$policy)
```

* **Stationary Thompson sampling** is excellent before the change (regret
  `r round(b[["thompson"]])`) and the worst policy after it
  (`r round(w[["thompson"]])`): its posterior on MCS20 is built from
  about 1,000 observations and takes a long time to be overturned.
* **Discounted Thompson sampling** trades the two phases off through
  `gamma`. With `gamma = 0.99` (memory of about 100 observations) it
  adapts after the change (`r round(w[["dts_0.99"]])`) but forgets too
  fast to settle beforehand (`r round(b[["dts_0.99"]])`). With
  `gamma = 0.998` (memory of about 500) the balance is
  `r round(b[["dts_0.998"]])` before and `r round(w[["dts_0.998"]])`
  after. `gamma` is a design parameter that should be matched to how
  fast the radio conditions actually change.
* **OLLA** is the most robust policy in this experiment
  (`r round(b[["olla"]])` before, `r round(w[["olla"]])` after). Its
  offset tracks a level shift within a few dozen NACKs. A bandit that
  is to replace OLLA on a live network has to beat this, which points
  to hybrid designs (for example, a bandit choosing OLLA's BLER target
  or step size per context) rather than a bandit choosing MCS directly.

## 6. What this shows about banditlab, and what it needs next

What worked without modifying the package:

* Arbitrary radio-link reward models via `bandit_custom()` and new
  environment classes.
* Industry baselines (a CQI table, OLLA) and two literature policies
  (binarised and discounted Thompson sampling) through the three-method
  extension API.
* Seed-paired replicated comparison, exact pseudo-regret for stationary
  problems, and plots that need no styling work.

Gaps that this case study exposed, in priority order for RAN use:

1. **Time-aware environments.** `sample_reward()` should receive the
   step `t`, and environments should be able to declare time-varying
   expected rewards so the engine can report dynamic regret. The clock
   workaround above is fragile.
2. **Non-binary Thompson sampling and non-stationary policies built in.**
   Most RAN rewards (throughput, SINR, energy per bit) are continuous,
   and network conditions drift on diurnal and weekly cycles. Gaussian
   or binarised Thompson sampling, discounted and sliding-window
   variants, and reward scaling checks for UCB1 (which assumes rewards
   in `[0, 1]`) belong in the package.
3. **Batched and delayed feedback.** Cell-level parameters (CIO, A3
   offset, time-to-trigger, tilt, reference signal power) are changed
   per cell and evaluated on counters aggregated over 15-minute or
   hourly reporting periods. The engine updates after every pull; a
   batch-update mode would match how network optimisation is actually
   run.
4. **Contextual policies.** Link adaptation and mobility tuning depend
   on context (CQI, load, speed, cell type). LinUCB and linear Thompson
   sampling, which the book's Part V covers, are the natural next
   policies.
5. **Safe exploration.** UCB1 and Thompson sampling try every MCS,
   including ones an engineer knows will fail. Constrained or
   conservative policies (never perform worse than a baseline by more
   than a margin) are what make bandits acceptable on a live network.
6. **Off-policy evaluation from network logs.** The trajectory log
   already records propensities for value-based policies; an inverse
   propensity or doubly robust estimator would let a new policy be
   evaluated on historical data before it touches a cell.

## References

* 3GPP TS 38.214, *NR; Physical layer procedures for data*, Table
  5.1.3.1-1.
* Agrawal, S. and Goyal, N. (2012). Analysis of Thompson sampling for
  the multi-armed bandit problem. *COLT*.
* Raj, V. and Kalyani, S. (2017). Taming non-stationary bandits: a
  Bayesian approach. arXiv:1707.09727.
* Lattimore, T. and Szepesvári, C. (2020). *Bandit Algorithms*.
  Cambridge University Press.
